extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers and practitioners working on computational humor detection and computational humor production
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, evaluating, or producing short-text humor detectors (and producing short jokes) using sentence-level BERT embeddings and parallel architectures that capture setup–punchline script relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Input text is split into its constituent sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clear sentence boundaries in inputs (and generated texts). The architecture assumes sentence-level units so texts without clear sentence segmentation are poorly modeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: BERT embedding per sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Each sentence is independently encoded with BERT, producing a fixed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encode sentences independently rather than pooling entire text; independent embeddings preserve sentence-level script information that pooling would destroy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel hidden layers (one channel per sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each sentence embedding feeds its own line of hidden layers (a parallel 'channel' per sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain separate downstream processing for each sentence to keep script-specific information separate before combining; this design choice underlies ColBERT's gains over single-channel models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concatenation and classification head
rubrics_metrics.description: The parallel channels' outputs are concatenated and passed to a final classification head which produces the humor label or score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine sentence-specific representations only after sentence-level processing; final classifier should leverage between-channel relations rather than relying on a single pooled vector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve script-level structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectures that preserve script-level structure outperform architectures that merge text into a single representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design models to preserve and compare sentence-level scripts (e.g., setup vs punchline) rather than collapsing all tokens into one representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script opposition / between-script relations (incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from the relation between sentence-level scripts (especially incongruity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detection should target contrasts or oppositions between scripts carried by different sentences (setup vs punchline) rather than only intra-sentence features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level incongruity detection
rubrics_metrics.description: The second/last sentence shifts the interpretive frame (i.e., a meaningful asymmetry between sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and exploit shifts in embedding-space between sentences; models should be sensitive to frame-shifting second/last sentences as key humor signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical surprise patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly low-frequency or phonetically marked words at punchline position are predictive of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place comic-significant or surprising lexical items at the punchline; model features should capture lexical distinctiveness and surprise at punchline positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural pattern features
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns such as length distributions, sentence count, and the ending position of comic load are useful signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structural features (e.g., number of sentences, punchline placement, length) as part of detection; comic load often concentrates near the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific markers and topical biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain topics or domain markers are frequently associated with jokes and can be learned by the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for domain/topic signals but beware of dataset-specific topical biases; distinguish genuine humor signals from topical confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset balancing and matched negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The released dataset contains 100,000 humorous and 100,000 non-humorous texts matched for length and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building/evaluating benchmarks, match non-humorous negatives on length/style to avoid trivial discriminative cues; use large, balanced datasets for robust evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability scope and limitation awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: The architecture works on short jokes with clear sentence-segmented setup–punchline format but struggles with long-form, subtle/ironic, or world-knowledge humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit claims to genres represented in training data (short, sentence-separated jokes). Expect degraded performance on long-form narratives, irony requiring pragmatic/world knowledge, or culturally specific humor absent from data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-sentence requirement for script detection
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is detectable to the extent that multiple sentences are present with internally coherent meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer inputs (or generated jokes) that include at least a setup and a punchline as separate sentences—single-sentence jokes may not exhibit separable scripts for this architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline embedding asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline sentence's embedding should be meaningfully different from the setup's (script asymmetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate embedding-distance or representational difference between setup and punchline as a diagnostic signal; ensure punchline distinctiveness in semantics/lexicon/structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate comic load at final sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic load is often concentrated in the final sentence (or last clause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating jokes for this model, place comic-significant material toward the end of the text so between-sentence comparisons capture the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical production/evaluation principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate or evaluate text with sentence boundaries clear; maintain setup–punchline asymmetry; place comic-significant words at the punchline; use sentence-separable scripts that contrast cleanly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these heuristics to craft data or synthetic jokes amenable to parallel-architecture detection; they are operational prescriptions derived from model behavior and theoretical framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic evaluation questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to check whether a text is analyzable by parallel-architecture humor detectors (e.g., Are sentences individually coherent under their own script? Do embeddings reflect asymmetry? Is comic load concentrated in the final sentence?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these diagnostic questions during data curation and model error analysis to identify why a model succeeded or failed on a given instance.
